pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset with circulatory and cellular/metabolic failure severe enough to raise mortality substantially (above 40% in hospital).
keyMechanisms: Dysregulated host response: the inflammatory and anti-inflammatory response to infection injures the patient's own organs, not just the infected site.
Organ dysfunction: identified as an acute rise in SOFA score of 2 or more (about 10% mortality in a general ward population with suspected infection).
Circulatory failure: vasodilation and capillary leak cause hypotension; tissue hypoperfusion raises lactate and slows capillary refill.
Septic shock: vasopressor needed to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg AND lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid.
Time matters: early antimicrobials are among the most effective ways to reduce mortality; observational data link delays beyond 3–5 h with higher mortality even without shock.

symptoms: Fever or rigors, or hypothermia; malaise.
Symptoms of the source: cough and sputum, dysuria and flank pain, abdominal pain, cellulitis, headache and neck stiffness, line or wound infection.
physicalSigns: Tachycardia, tachypnoea (RR 22 or more), hypotension (SBP 100 or less).
Mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill, cold peripheries.
Signs of the source: chest crackles, abdominal tenderness or peritonism, red hot skin, infected line site.
redFlags: Hypotension not responding to fluid, or rising lactate: septic shock; start vasopressor and call ICU
Any qSOFA criterion (RR 22 or more, altered mentation, SBP 100 or less) is a prompt to assess for sepsis, but SSC recommends against qSOFA as a single screening tool
Needs emergency source control: necrotising soft-tissue infection, obstructed infected kidney, perforation, abscess, infected device
precipitants: Pneumonia, urinary tract, intra-abdominal, skin and soft tissue, CNS and line-related infections.
Higher risk: older age, diabetes, immunosuppression, chronic kidney or liver disease, cancer, recent surgery or invasive devices.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Clear non-infectious trigger; cultures negative. SSC: reassess daily and stop antibiotics if an alternative cause is shown.
Cold, wet, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, poor ventricular function on echo; ischaemic ECG or raised troponin.
Bleeding or fluid loss; falling haemoglobin; responds to volume.
Sudden breathlessness, hypoxia, right heart strain; risk factors for VTE.
Allergen exposure with urticaria or angioedema; or steroid withdrawal with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: At presentation; repeat to guide resuscitation if raised
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Above 2 mmol/L (with vasopressor need = septic shock).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: SSC suggests measuring lactate and guiding resuscitation to bring a raised lactate down; interpret with other causes of raised lactate in mind.

ruleIn.testName: FBC, U&E and creatinine, bilirubin, platelets, coagulation, blood gas
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Creatinine rise or oliguria; bilirubin rise; platelets falling; PaO2/FiO2 falling.

ruleIn.normalValue: Creatinine 60–110 µmol/L; bilirubin below 21 µmol/L; platelets 150–400 × 10⁹/L

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and start immediately
actions: Sepsis and septic shock are emergencies: begin treatment and resuscitation immediately.
Screen acutely ill patients with a tool such as NEWS, MEWS or SIRS; do not rely on qSOFA alone.
Measure lactate; send blood cultures before antibiotics if this does not delay them.

clinicalManagement.title: Antimicrobials
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 h if shock or high likelihood of sepsis
actions: Septic shock or high likelihood of sepsis: give antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 h of recognition.
Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment for infection vs other causes; if concern persists, antimicrobials within 3 h.
Choose by likely source and local antibiogram (MOH LRTI, UTI and intra-abdominal infection protocols). Add MRSA cover only if high MRSA risk; two Gram-negative agents only if high MDR risk.
Give beta-lactams as a prolonged infusion after an initial bolus; dose by PK/PD principles.
Empiric antifungal therapy (SSC suggests).

branches.condition: Low likelihood of infection and no shock
actions: Defer antimicrobials and monitor closely.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid resuscitation
actions: Sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock: at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid within the first 3 h.
Balanced crystalloid preferred to 0.9% saline; consider albumin after large crystalloid volumes; avoid starches and gelatin.
Reassess after each bolus with dynamic measures (passive leg raise, stroke volume), capillary refill and lactate.

clinicalManagement.title: Vasopressors to MAP 65
clinicalManagement.timeframe: If hypotension persists during or after fluids
actions: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) first-line; start peripherally (short term, vein at or above the antecubital fossa) rather than waiting for a central line.
Target MAP 65 mmHg initially. Arterial line as soon as practical.

branches.condition: MAP still inadequate on noradrenaline 0.25–0.5 microgram/kg/min
actions: Add vasopressin rather than escalating noradrenaline.
Add adrenaline (epinephrine).

branches.condition: Cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP
actions: Add dobutamine to noradrenaline, or use adrenaline alone.

branches.condition: Ongoing vasopressor need (noradrenaline or adrenaline at least 0.25 microgram/kg/min for at least 4 h)
actions: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg IV every 6 h or infusion).

clinicalManagement.title: Source control and level of care
actions: Drain abscesses, debride infected tissue, relieve obstruction; remove infected intravascular devices after new access is established.
Patients needing ICU: admit within 6 h.
Hypoxaemic respiratory failure: high-flow nasal oxygen rather than NIV.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing care
actions: Reassess daily for antibiotic de-escalation; use the shortest effective course once the source is controlled.
Start insulin if glucose is 10 mmol/L or more (target 8–10 mmol/L).
Restrictive transfusion (trigger haemoglobin 70 g/L in most patients).
Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis (LMWH preferred); stress ulcer prophylaxis if risk factors for GI bleeding.
Do not give IV vitamin C; no bicarbonate for lactic acidosis unless pH 7.2 or less with AKI stage 2–3.

adjustments: Smaller boluses with careful reassessment in heart or kidney failure
Albumin if large crystalloid volumes needed; no starches or gelatin
monitoring: Dynamic measures, capillary refill, lactate, urine output

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with MAP below 65 despite fluids
regimens.dose: Titrate to MAP 65 mmHg (SSC gives no fixed dose)
regimens.route: IV; peripheral short term, then central
adjustments: Peripheral only short term, at or above the antecubital fossa

regimens.indication: Septic shock not at target on noradrenaline
regimens.dose: Add rather than escalating noradrenaline (SSC gives no fixed dose; follow local protocol)
adjustments: Third agent if still inadequate: adrenaline

regimens.indication: Septic shock with ongoing vasopressor need
regimens.patientGroup: Noradrenaline or adrenaline at least 0.25 microgram/kg/min for at least 4 h
regimens.dose: 200 mg/day: 50 mg every 6 h or continuous infusion
regimens.duration: Until vasopressors are no longer needed (local protocol for taper)

medicationPlan.note: Fluid, vasopressor and steroid doses are as stated in SSC 2021. Empiric antibiotic choice depends on the source: use the Saudi MOH LRTI, UTI and intra-abdominal infection protocols and the local antibiogram.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Suspected or confirmed infection + acute rise in SOFA score of 2 or more
Vasopressor needed for MAP at least 65 mmHg AND lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation
RR 22 or more, altered mentation, SBP 100 or less — not a stand-alone screening tool

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage sepsis and septic shock in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Waiting for cultures or imaging before giving antibiotics in shock.
Using qSOFA alone to rule sepsis out.
Delaying vasopressors until a central line is in.
Forgetting source control (pus, obstruction, infected line).
keyPoints: Antimicrobials within 1 h in septic shock; within 3 h if possible sepsis without shock.
30 mL/kg crystalloid in the first 3 h for hypoperfusion; balanced crystalloid preferred.
Noradrenaline first; MAP 65; add vasopressin at 0.25–0.5 microgram/kg/min.
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day if vasopressors are still needed.
